title: Assignability, subtyping, and excess property checks
hook: TypeScript decides whether one type can stand in for another using structural rules — if the shape fits, the assignment works. That sounds simple until extra properties, readonly flags, and unions enter the picture.

blocks.text: **Assignability** asks: can a value of type **Source** be used where type **Target** is expected? TypeScript uses **structural subtyping** — Source is assignable to Target if Source has at least all the properties Target requires, with compatible types. This differs from C#'s **nominal** system where only declared inheritance relationships matter. **Excess property checks** apply to fresh object literals: extra properties not in the target type cause an error, even when the variable would otherwise be structurally compatible. Function parameter checking is **bivariant** for methods in older modes but **strictFunctionTypes** makes parameters contravariant — a senior interview topic.

entries.plainDefinition: A type is a subtype of another if its shape is compatible — extra properties on the value are often OK when assigning through a variable.
entries.example: `{ name: string; age: number }` assignable to `{ name: string }`.

entries.plainDefinition: When you pass an object literal directly, TypeScript rejects unknown properties not declared on the target type.
entries.example: `const u: User = { name: "Ada", extra: 1 }` — error on `extra`.

entries.plainDefinition: A newly written `{ ... }` expression subject to stricter excess property rules than a variable reference.
entries.example: Assign through a variable first to bypass excess check — usually a code smell.

blocks.text: Misunderstanding assignability causes false confidence: you think a wider API type is safe because C# would have blocked it. Union assignability is directional — `"a"` fits `string` but not the reverse. Excess property checks catch typos in config objects (`{ naem: "x" }` would otherwise silently match a partial type). For C# developers, structural typing is the biggest mental model shift in TypeScript.

blocks.title: Variable vs literal
blocks.body: Excess property checks apply to **fresh** object literals, not to variables already typed wider. `const x = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const y: { a: number } = x` is allowed — `x` is not fresh at the assignment point.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Required properties present
items.body: Target's required keys must exist on Source with assignable types.

items.title: Optionality compatible
items.body: An optional target property can be missing on Source. Required Source properties cannot be optional on Target unless types align.

items.title: Union direction
items.body: Source union must be assignable to Target union member-by-member. A single literal assigns to a wider union.

items.title: Excess check on literals
items.body: Direct `{ ... }` to typed parameter — no extra keys allowed beyond index signatures.

diagram.title: Structural assignability

snippet.label: Structural subtyping — extra properties OK via variable
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–4: intersection defines the full shape. Lines 6–11: object literal with an extra `id` is allowed when the target type includes all required fields (excess check may still warn if target is exact). Line 13: assigning wider variable to narrower `Point` is valid — only `x` and `y` are required.

snippet.label: Excess property check on fresh literal
snippet.explanation: Line 8: excess property check catches the typo/extra field immediately. Lines 10–11: when the object is stored in a variable first, TypeScript compares structurally and allows extra properties — intentional escape hatch, not a feature to abuse.

snippet.label: Union assignability direction
snippet.explanation: Lines 4–5: assigning a narrower literal to a wider union is safe. Lines 7–8: reverse is unsafe — `wide` might be `"done"`. Lines 10–11: passing a union where a single literal is required fails.

snippet.label: readonly blocks assignment to mutable
snippet.explanation: Lines 6–7: you cannot assign readonly to mutable — mutation would break the readonly contract. Lines 9–10: the opposite direction works — readonly consumers accept mutable data.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming C# nominal rules apply — unrelated classes with the same shape are assignable in TS. Relying on the variable workaround to smuggle misspelled keys. Expecting union assignability to work both directions.

blocks.text: With `strictFunctionTypes`, function parameters are checked contravariantly for callbacks — a subtle source of generic bugs. **Optional properties** vs `| undefined` differ under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. Intersection assignability requires each constituent to be assignable. For API evolution, prefer explicit DTO types over anonymous shapes to get excess property protection. Branding (module 15) restores nominal-like safety when needed.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Calling TypeScript nominal. Not explaining excess property checks vs structural widening. Reversing union assignability. Unaware that readonly is covariant but mutable is not assignable from readonly.

interviewTakeaways: TypeScript subtyping is structural — compatible shape means assignable.
Excess property checks apply to fresh object literals, not widened variables.
Union assignability is directional: narrow assigns to wide, not always reverse.
readonly types are assignable from mutable, not the other way around.
60s: TS asks 'does the shape fit?' C# asks 'is it declared?' Excess checks catch typos on literals. Unions narrow-to-wide only.
commonPitfalls: Expecting C# nominal inheritance rules in TypeScript.
Smuggling extra keys through an intermediate variable to silence excess errors.
Strong answer: 'Structural subtyping. Fresh literals get excess checks. readonly covariance. C# needs explicit interface implementation.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has always been structural at runtime ('if it quacks...'). TypeScript formalizes that into compile-time assignability rules.
C# requires explicit inheritance or interface implementation. Two unrelated classes with identical fields are not interchangeable.
